The rise of tobacco as the cash crop of the Colony of Virginia, starting in 1612. That year the colonist John Rolfe planted a sweeter tobacco from Caribbean seed at Jamestown, instead of the harsh local kind. The first crop reached England in 1614 and sold well.

Tobacco saved the struggling colony and shaped it:

  • Planters spread out along the rivers, taking land from the Powhatan peoples.
  • They needed labour, first indentured servants from England, then enslaved Africans; the first Africans arrived in 1619.
  • Tobacco wore out the soil fast, so planters kept moving west.
  • Tobacco leaf itself was used as money.

Tobacco was one of the great American gifts of the Columbian Exchange. Within about a century of 1492, people smoked it from England to the Ottoman Empire, India, China and Japan. Virginia and Maryland became Britain's main suppliers, and tobacco was the heart of British North America's southern economy until cotton.
